# Three Columns Answer Three Different Questions

An RNA-seq differential-expression table commonly places a log2 fold change,
p-value, and adjusted p-value on the same row. They are related, but they are not
interchangeable:

| Quantity | Main question | What it does not answer |
|---|---|---|
| Log2 fold change | How large and in which direction is the modeled contrast? | How precise is it? |
| P-value | How incompatible is the test statistic with a specified null model? | What is the probability the null is true? |
| Adjusted p-value or q-value | How strong is the evidence after accounting for a testing family? | Is the effect biologically important? |
| Confidence interval | Which effect sizes are compatible with the data and model? | Which value is most biologically plausible without context? |

A small p-value can accompany a tiny but precise effect. A large estimated fold
change can come from a few unstable counts and have weak evidence. A low FDR does
not turn an association into a causal mechanism. Interpretation begins by defining
the contrast and scale, then reading magnitude, uncertainty, and multiplicity
together.

# The Effect Estimand Comes First

For gene $g$ and sample $j$, a negative-binomial generalized linear model may use

$$
K_{gj}\sim\operatorname{NB}(\mu_{gj},\alpha_g),
\qquad
\log(\mu_{gj})=\log(s_j)+\mathbf x_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta_g.
$$

Here $s_j$ is a normalization factor, $\mathbf x_j$ is a design row, and
$\boldsymbol\beta_g$ contains gene-specific coefficients. For a contrast vector
$\mathbf c$, the natural-log contrast is $\theta_g=\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}
\boldsymbol\beta_g$. Software often reports

$$
\operatorname{LFC}_g=\frac{\theta_g}{\log 2}
=\log_2\left(\frac{\text{modeled expression in numerator condition}}
{\text{modeled expression in denominator condition}}
\right).
$$

Thus $\operatorname{LFC}=1$ represents a twofold ratio, $-1$ a one-half ratio,
and $0$ no modeled difference. The meaning changes with the contrast:

- in a two-group model, it may compare treatment with control;
- with a continuous predictor, it is the change per one-unit predictor increase;
- with an interaction, it is a difference between condition effects;
- with covariates, it is a conditional model coefficient, not automatically a
  marginal population average;
- after a transformation or alternative parameterization, the coefficient may no
  longer be a simple ratio of raw group means.

Always report the numerator, denominator, units, coefficient or contrast, covariate
adjustment, and target population. A sign without a declared contrast direction is
not interpretable.

# Estimate, Standard Error, and Test

Let $\hat\theta_g$ estimate the contrast and let
$\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta_g)$ quantify its sampling variability. A
Wald statistic for the point null $H_{0g}:\theta_g=0$ is

$$
Z_g=\frac{\hat\theta_g}{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta_g)},
$$

with a two-sided large-sample p-value

$$
p_g=2\left\{1-\Phi(|Z_g|)\right\}.
$$

The p-value depends on both magnitude and precision. Two genes can have the same
fold change but different p-values because one has more counts, lower dispersion,
more independent samples, or a better-estimated contrast. Conversely, a very small
effect can have a small p-value in a large, precise study.

The p-value is calculated assuming the null model and the analysis pipeline. It is
not $P(H_{0g}\mid\text{data})$, the probability that chance created the result, or
the probability that a replication will agree. Model misspecification, confounding,
pseudoreplication, or underestimated dispersion can make it anti-conservative.

# From P-values to FDR

When thousands of genes are tested, interpreting each p-value at 0.05 ignores the
number of opportunities for false positives. The false discovery proportion is

$$
\operatorname{FDP}=\frac{V}{\max(R,1)},
$$

where $R$ is the number of rejected hypotheses and $V$ the unknown number of false
rejections. The FDR is $E(\operatorname{FDP})$ over repeated realizations of the
complete procedure.

The BH-adjusted p-value for a gene is the smallest BH target level at which that gene
would be rejected within the declared family. Software sometimes labels this value
`FDR` or `qvalue`, but Storey's q-values use an additional estimate of the proportion
of true nulls. Name the procedure rather than inferring it from a column heading.

An FDR threshold of 0.05 does not mean that every reported gene has a 95% probability
of being truly differential, nor does it guarantee that exactly 5% of one list is
false. The guarantee concerns the expected false discovery proportion of the full
selection procedure under its assumptions.

# Fold-change Uncertainty and Shrinkage

Low counts or high dispersion can produce extremely variable maximum-likelihood
fold-change estimates. A pseudocount such as

$$
\log_2\left(\frac{\bar K_{g1}+a}{\bar K_{g0}+a}\right)
$$

prevents division by zero but makes the result depend arbitrarily on $a$, ignores
the design, and does not propagate uncertainty. Model-based shrinkage instead uses
information across genes to pull noisy estimates toward a prior center, usually
zero, while allowing well-supported effects to move less.

DESeq2, apeglm, and adaptive shrinkage methods can provide stabilized effects for
ranking and visualization. Heavy-tailed priors aim to retain genuinely large
effects while shrinking weakly informed estimates. Shrinkage changes the estimator,
not the raw data. Report which estimator is shown and do not combine a shrunken
effect from one procedure with a p-value whose null and coefficient came from a
different, undocumented analysis.

A shrunken estimate near zero does not prove no effect; it says the data provide
limited information after regularization. An unshrunken, enormous low-count estimate
does not prove a large biological effect; its interval may span a wide range.

# Testing a Scientifically Meaningful Effect

The usual null $H_0:\theta_g=0$ asks whether the effect is exactly zero. It does not
test whether the effect exceeds a biologically important threshold $\delta$. To seek
effects meaningfully different from zero, test the composite null

$$
H_{0g}:|\theta_g|\leq\delta
\qquad\text{against}\qquad
H_{1g}:|\theta_g|>\delta.
$$

TREAT and related count-model procedures implement tests relative to a fold-change
threshold. Such p-values are typically larger than point-null p-values because the
claim is stronger. The threshold should be chosen from biological resolution, assay
performance, intervention costs, or a decision context before seeing results.

Applying the rule `adjusted p-value < 0.05 and observed |LFC| > 1` is not equivalent
to testing $|\theta_g|>1$. The first step tests a zero effect and then filters on a
noisy estimate; it does not provide an error guarantee for effects exceeding the
threshold. If the scientific question concerns a minimum effect, put that threshold
inside the hypothesis or use intervals to show whether the threshold is supported.

The reverse question also matters. To argue that an effect is negligibly small,
use an equivalence test or an interval contained within $[-\delta,\delta]$. A large
p-value for the point null does not establish equivalence.

# A Worked Interpretation

Suppose a treatment-versus-control analysis reports:

| Gene | Log2 fold change | Standard error | Raw p-value | BH adjusted p-value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 0.20 | 0.04 | $5.7\times10^{-7}$ | $0.002$ |
| B | 2.10 | 1.15 | $0.068$ | $0.31$ |
| C | -1.30 | 0.22 | $3.4\times10^{-9}$ | $0.00003$ |

- Gene A has strong statistical evidence for a precisely estimated but small
  modeled change: $2^{0.20}\approx1.15$, about a 15% ratio increase. Whether that is
  biologically important requires context.
- Gene B has a large point estimate, about a $2^{2.10}\approx4.3$-fold ratio, but
  high uncertainty. It is a candidate for more information, not evidence of a
  reliably large change.
- Gene C combines a large negative estimate, about a $2^{-1.30}\approx0.41$ ratio,
  with strong evidence after multiplicity adjustment. Its mechanism and biological
  relevance still require validation.

These interpretations assume the contrast, normalization, dispersion model, and
experimental-unit structure are valid. The table alone cannot establish causality,
functional importance, or transportability.

# Volcano and MA Plots

A volcano plot displays effect estimate against $-\log_{10}(p)$ or adjusted p-value.
It is useful for seeing the distinction between magnitude and evidence, but it can
also encourage threshold worship and selective labeling. Points are not independent
biological replicates, and the upper corners are not automatically the best targets.

An MA plot displays log fold change against mean abundance. It reveals abundance-
dependent variability, low-count extremes, and the effect of shrinkage. Plot raw or
normalized counts for important genes so that one outlier or a small subgroup is not
hidden by a summary point.

Plot annotations should state whether fold changes are maximum-likelihood or
shrunken, whether the vertical quantity is raw or adjusted evidence, and which
thresholds were applied. Label selection is part of communication and should not
silently become a new inferential procedure.

# Experimental Units and Biological Interpretation

For bulk RNA-seq, the experimental units are usually independently sampled donors,
organisms, or cultures. Libraries, lanes, and reads are technical observations. In
single-cell studies, cells are ordinarily nested within biological samples; treating
every cell as an independent replicate can produce tiny p-values without independent
biological evidence.

Technical replication can reduce measurement error or reveal assay failure, but
biological replication estimates variation across the population to which inference
is intended. FDR correction cannot repair standard errors computed from the wrong
unit. Likewise, thousands of discoveries from a confounded treatment/batch design
may be statistically stable associations with batch rather than treatment effects.

Statistical interpretation should state the modeled population contrast, estimate,
uncertainty, and multiplicity procedure. Biological interpretation asks whether the
change is plausible, meaningful on the relevant scale, coherent with orthogonal
evidence, and reproducible in independent samples. Pathway membership or a familiar
gene name does not substitute for these checks.

# Diagnostics and Sensitivity

| Issue | Why it matters | Check or response |
|---|---|---|
| Contrast coding | Reverses signs or changes the estimand | Print coefficient names and the exact contrast |
| Low counts | Produces unstable effects and discrete evidence | Inspect counts, intervals, MA plots, and shrinkage |
| Outliers | A single sample can dominate both effect and test | Inspect sample-level counts and influence diagnostics |
| Normalization failure | Global composition shifts distort ratios | Compare defensible factors and use controls when available |
| Dispersion/model failure | Miscalibrates standard errors and p-values | Residual checks, mean--variance diagnostics, simulation |
| Hidden batch or confounding | Changes the meaning of the coefficient | Audit metadata, randomization, balance, and design rank |
| Filtering and family definition | Changes adjusted values and FDR scope | Report all feature counts and the filtering rule |
| Effect estimator | Raw and shrunken LFCs answer different estimation questions | State estimator and compare uncertainty-aware rankings |

Sensitivity analyses should vary justified normalization, dispersion, filtering,
outlier, and shrinkage choices. Conclusions stable in direction and scientifically
relevant magnitude are stronger than conclusions defined only by crossing 0.05 in
one pipeline.

# Reporting Checklist

Report enough information to reconstruct the meaning of every result:

1. biological system, target population, and independent experimental units;
2. group sizes at the biological-unit level and relevant technical nesting;
3. count generation, annotation, eligibility, and prefiltering rules;
4. normalization, design formula, coefficient or contrast, and reference levels;
5. fold-change scale and whether estimates are raw or shrunken;
6. test type, null hypothesis, effect threshold if any, and uncertainty interval;
7. multiple-testing family, adjustment method, independent filtering, and target FDR;
8. numbers eligible, fitted, tested, retained after filtering, and rejected;
9. diagnostics, sensitivity analyses, and validation evidence;
10. separate statistical and biological conclusions.

# Common Misinterpretations

- **“Fold change is effect certainty.”** It is a point estimate; read it with its
  uncertainty and information level.
- **“P < 0.05 means a 95% chance of a real effect.”** A p-value is a tail probability
  under a null model, not a posterior probability.
- **“FDR 5% means this gene has a 5% false-positive probability.”** FDR is an expected
  property of a discovery procedure, not usually a gene-specific posterior.
- **“Not significant means no effect.”** It may mean insufficient information; use
  intervals or equivalence tests for absence claims.
- **“Significant means important.”** Biological importance requires an effect scale,
  threshold, context, and validation.
- **“A twofold cutoff fixes multiplicity.”** An estimate cutoff does not replace a
  valid hypothesis test or FDR procedure.
- **“More reads are more biological replicates.”** Depth improves measurement but
  does not sample more independent biological units.

# Connections and Take-home Messages

- [Differential-expression contrasts and design matrices](differential-expression-contrasts-and-design-matrices.qmd) defines the estimand and contrast direction.
- [Negative-binomial differential-expression models](negative-binomial-differential-expression-models.qmd) derives the count likelihood and gene-wise tests.
- [Dispersion estimation and shrinkage](dispersion-estimation-and-shrinkage-in-rna-seq.qmd) explains how RNA-seq uncertainty is moderated.
- [Independent filtering and RNA-seq multiple testing](independent-filtering-and-rna-seq-multiple-testing.qmd) shows how the tested family is selected before FDR adjustment.
- [Effect sizes](../statistical-inference/effect-sizes.qmd) separates magnitude from evidence and causality.
- [Null distributions and p-values](../statistical-inference/null-distributions-and-p-values.qmd) gives the repeated-sampling interpretation of a p-value.
- [False discovery rate](../statistical-inference/false-discovery-rate.qmd) distinguishes FDR, local FDR, and the realized false discovery proportion.
- [Statistical versus practical significance](../statistical-inference/statistical-versus-practical-significance.qmd) connects effect thresholds to decisions.
- [Biological versus technical replication](biological-versus-technical-replication.qmd) identifies the units that determine inferential precision.

Fold changes describe modeled magnitude and direction; p-values describe evidence
against a declared null; FDR procedures describe repeated-study error among selected
hypotheses. None replaces the others. Reliable RNA-seq interpretation combines a
clear contrast, an uncertainty-aware effect estimate, valid gene-wise tests, a
declared multiple-testing family, correct experimental units, and biological
validation.
